the value of CD4 and VL testing for tailoring ART monitoring strategies in resource limited settings is limited.
the use of POC CD4 and VL testing is feasible and cost-effective in tailoring ART initiation and monitoring strategies in resource-limited settings.
the use of point-of-care CD4 testing in the routine management of HIV-infected adults in resource-limited settings may not lead to significant improvements in patient care.

developing and evaluating an approach to the problem of tailoring monitoring strategies to resource limitations.
the development of a new approach to HIV monitoring and treatment.
the development and evaluation of a point-of-care (POC) CD4 test, and the use of CD4 testing and viral load monitoring to inform ART monitoring strategies in resource limited settings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no evidence to suggest that a single point-of-care CD4 test is more accurate than the current laboratory CD4 test in the diagnosis of HIV disease.
, while the use of POC CD4 testing is feasible in resource-limited settings, it does not appear to offer any advantages over the use of laboratory-based CD4 testing.

the value of POC CD4 and laboratory viral load in tailoring ART strategies to resource limitations is still unclear.
the value of CD4 and VL monitoring is dependent on the level of resource constraints, and that the most important resource is human resources.

point-of-care CD4 and viral load monitoring is a viable option for resource-limited countries to monitor HIV patients on ART.
we can use point-of-care CD4 and viral load tests in resource-limited settings to tailor ART monitoring strategies and improve the cost-effectiveness of care.
